hints: Remember stereoisomerism means either E/Z isomerism around a C=C bond or optical isomerism at a chiral centre, so check each molecule for those two features.
For the two propenes, look closely at each carbon of the double bond and ask if both carbons carry two different groups.
For the two propanes, draw out $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl-CHCl-CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{Cl}$ and see which carbon has four different groups attached.
walkthrough:
**Recall the two types of stereoisomerism**

There are two main types you need at AS Level. Alkenes can show E/Z (cis-trans) isomerism, and saturated molecules can show optical isomerism if they have a chiral centre.

Rule to use:
$$\text{chiral carbon = carbon with 4 different groups}$$

**Test the alkenes for E/Z isomerism**

For E/Z you need each C of the C=C to have two different substituents. Draw them out simply.

$$\text{A: CCl}_2\text{=CH-CH}_3 \quad \text{B: CH}_2\text{=C(Cl)-CH}_2\text{Cl}$$

In A, C1 has two Cl atoms identical. In B, C1 has two H atoms identical. So neither alkene can show E/Z isomerism, and neither has a chiral $sp^3$ carbon either.

**Test the alkanes for optical isomerism**

Now look at the saturated compounds.

$$\text{C: CH}_2\text{Cl-CHCl-CH}_3 \quad \text{D: CH}_2\text{Cl-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{Cl}$$

In D, every carbon has at least two H atoms, so no chiral centre. In C, look at C2. It is bonded to H, Cl, $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$, four different groups. That is a chiral centre, so C shows optical stereoisomerism as a pair of enantiomers.

options.A: Incorrect. 1,1-dichloropropene is $\text{CCl}_2\text{=CH-CH}_3$. C1 of the double bond carries two identical Cl atoms, so E/Z isomerism is impossible. There is also no chiral single-bonded carbon.
options.B: Incorrect. 2,3-dichloropropene is $\text{CH}_2\text{=C(Cl)-CH}_2\text{Cl}$. C1 of the double bond carries two identical H atoms, so E/Z isomerism is impossible. C3 has two H atoms and C2 is $sp^2$, so there is no chiral centre either.
options.C: Correct. 1,2-dichloropropane is $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl-CHCl-CH}_3$. Carbon 2 is attached to H, Cl, $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$, which are four different groups. It is chiral and exists as two non-superimposable optical isomers (enantiomers).
options.D: Incorrect. 1,3-dichloropropane is $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{Cl}$. It is symmetrical with no C=C bond and no carbon with four different groups, so it shows neither E/Z nor optical isomerism.
